chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
title: The wartime slump in recording and swing 'nipped'
summary: Poor material and the recording ban; Maxine says swing was nipped during the war.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: The later years of World War II I suppose you'd say. It just occurred to me today that Billie Holiday for instance, she stopped making, she made some songs from Milt Gabler in '42 and then she went over to, what was it, DecCar?
Yeah. So far as recordings are concerned there were, there might have been some
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
records made but they were poor. You had poor material, you know, the material that recordings were made out of was just not available.

During this time in the '40s that I made that album with I thought was a terrific album, the one with Ellis Larkins and the trio. And the material in the recording itself was so poor that the disc jockeys couldn't play it. The needle just skipped all over the place. And there were a lot of people not recording because even the recording companies were standing at a standstill. So they didn't have the material to make the record with. There's a possibility, I'm not sure but a lot of stuff that was being played was either transcriptions, I mean if you heard it on the radio, either transcriptions or old records. If there was stuff being sold in the stores, I mean, it didn't matter because the records wouldn't last that long anyway. So it was a quick thing. It was rough for everybody.
And there was the combination of both, the ASCAP thing.
Oh yeah, and then you had the
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Plus the recording band after that so the industry was in a kind of upheaval.
And I guess musically things were happening too because in some kind of way I suppose Swing was winding down.

Yeah well you see I always say swing was nipped, because during the war, when the war broke out bands began to break up because the musicians were being drafted and the bands were just having a hard time getting the same sound. They had to break in new musicians and had to start all over again. And of course also during that time there was a sort of a mass production of mediocre stuff, any kind of stuff because I imagine that the mood of the Country the way people were feeling - except other types. And you had alot of songs that came out during the war, the war sentiment. And some good songs came out. It was the times, so to speak. Getting back to staying number one, it's always a struggle. It is a struggle to get in and it's a struggle to stay there. But there are people, there are performers that
